column5: Employment Targets

Continue setting project employment targets for women at all 
J. 
levels as this is effective in keeping attention focused on the 
issue. There is a need to set minimum qualifications required 
for different posts—to allow the hiring of women. Government 
quotas may need upward revision. Stereotypes about what jobs 
women are suitable need to be gradually changed and women 
supported to break them by providing safe and comfortable 
working environments.

column7:
New or upgraded urban water supply, 
sanitation, and waste disposal
• 	Better	reflection	of	women’s	
priorities in selection of 
infrastructure investments
• 	More	women-friendly	design	and	
placement of infrastructure and 
increased personal safety
• 	Decreased	workloads	and	time	spent	
for women to meet household water 
and sanitation needs
column8:
• 	What	do	women	identify	as	their	
water and sanitation needs and 
priorities? How does this compare 
with men’s?
• 	What	are	women’s	views	on	issues	
such as number and location of 
facilities (pumps, toilets); sharing  
vs. individual facilities; types of 
latrines; etc.?
• 	Are	women’s	voices	in	community	
discussions and decision-making 
about water supply and sanitation 
adequate to meet their extensive 
household responsibilities for water 
and hygiene?
column9:
• 	Ensure	that	consultations	identify	
issues of women and men separately 
to better respond to needs.
• 	Give	priority	to	women’s	views	
for type, design, and location of 
household or community water 
supply, toilet facilities, and waste 
collection.
• 	Emphasize	separate	toilet	
provisions for women in low-income 
communities.

column7:
Increased access to water and 
sanitation supply with improved 
service standards. 
• 	More	households	with	connections,	
decreasing demands on women’s 
time and effort
• 	Better	conditions	for	women’s	
personal dignity and safety
column8:
• 	Has	the	approach	to	service	delivery	
in poor and slum areas considered 
how to overcome obstacles that poor 
households could face, particularly 
the lack of formal title or tenure to 
their dwelling?
• 	What	are	the	safety	issues	related	to	
location of water points and design 
and location of latrines that could  
be addressed through project plans 
and designs?
column9:
• 	Explore	options	to	ensure	that	
procedures for connection, billing, 
and payment do not exclude poor 
women and poor households.
• 	Consider	the	potential	for	policy	
reform to delink service provision 
to households from tenure 
arrangements.
• 	Where	toilets	are	not	private,	design	
and locate them so that women can 
reach and use them safely.

column7:
Expanded employment and income 
opportunities associated with new 
facilities and services
• 	Equitable	access	to	employment	
and income opportunities generated 
in management, delivery, or 
maintenance of new and  
upgraded services
• 	Improved	opportunities,	
productivity, and incomes  
for women
column8:
• 	What	are	the	opportunities	for	
employment related to management 
of new facilities (e.g., monitoring of 
functioning, or metering and billing 
processes)? Or in maintenance of 
new facilities (e.g., cleaning, repair)?
• 	What	types	of	work	do	women	do	
(considering casual labor, domestic 
service, market trading, home-based 
production, etc.)?
column9:
• 	Encourage	municipal	authorities	
managing new facilities to target 
women for training and employment 
in community-based management 
and maintenance.
• 	Consider	the	potential	to	involve	
women’s enterprises or self-help 
groups for management of tasks 
such as meter reading, billing, 
or consumer information, or for 
maintenance tasks.

column8:
• 	What	are	the	specific	constraints	
faced by women in slum areas in 
finding and keeping adequate jobs 
and incomes? Are these related to 
the context (e.g., transport options, 
time demands of inadequate 
services, limited employment on 
offer)? What are the constraints 
related to capacities (e.g., literacy, 
vocational, or management  
skills, etc.)?
• 	If	involvement	of	self-help	groups	is	
envisaged, what are their strengths 
and weaknesses? What are their 
livelihood activities? What is the 
potential to form viable affinity-
based groups?
column9:
• 	Partner	with	nongovernment	
organizations to develop programs 
for skills training, entrepreneurship 
training, and support.
• 	If	self-help	groups	are	part	of	the	
project livelihoods strategy, ensure 
that the project allocates the support 
necessary to form and/or sustain 
viable groups.
• 	Increase	linkages	of	women	and	
women’s self-help groups to 
government programs supporting 
livelihoods (skill training, 
entrepreneurship support).

column7:
Employment arising from project 
construction work
• 	Equitable	access	to	temporary	
project jobs
• 	Better	recognition	of	women’s	
rights to equal pay and appropriate 
working conditions
column8:
• 	Are	women	active	in	the	
construction sector in the project 
area? How do skill and pay levels 
compare with men’s?
• 	Are	workers	and	employers	and/
or contractors aware of core labor 
standards and workers’ rights, 
including women’s rights to 
nondiscrimination and equal pay?
column9:
• 	Set	targets	for	women’s	participation	
at different skill levels that are 
meaningful and achievable (given 
labor supply, local conditions, etc.).
• 	Brief	contractors	on	their	
responsibilities for equitable pay and 
working conditions.

column7:
Effective citizen participation in  
urban planning process, slum 
redevelopment planning, and other 
community committees
• 	Increased	opportunities	for	
women to voice their interests and 
participate in decision-making
• 	Increased	capacity	of	men	in	the	
community to work productively 
with women
• 	Support	to	minority	communities	
and those with special needs
column8:
• 	What	are	the	gender	dynamics	of	
participation in this locality? For 
example, are women equitably 
represented, do they have the 
opportunity or the confidence to 
voice their views, do men listen, 
and do women’s views influence 
discussions and decisions?
• 	Do	men	accept	women’s	
participation in these committees 
and support decisions that provide 
benefits to women?
column9:
• 	Work	with	municipal	authorities	
to ensure that citizen participation 
plans respond to the identified 
constraints on women’s participation 
(e.g., times and locations that 
allow women to attend, focus 
groups with women if there are 
difficulties in participating in mixed 
groups, supporting men to work 
constructively with women).

column7:
Strengthened governance capacity and 
practices of urban local bodies (elected 
members and staff )
• 	Elected	representatives	and	staff	
better informed about the needs of 
women in the areas they serve
• 	More	informed	and	skilled	women	
councilors and ward members
• 	Employment	of	female	in	the	lower	
grade jobs, e.g., cleaners.
column8:
• 	How	do	male	councilors	and	ward	
members see their responsibilities to 
women citizens, as users of services 
and as citizens?
• 	Do	poor	women	have	access	
to committee members and/or 
councilors?
• 	Are	elected	women	participating	in	
and chairing key ward and council 
committees? If not, why not?
column9:
• 	Partner	with	women’s	advocacy	
organizations to provide training to 
elected officials (both women and 
men) about women’s issues in  
the municipality.
• 	Facilitate	linkages	with	government	
programs to train women councilors.
• 	Facilitate	linkages	and	networking	
with elected women in other 
municipalities to exchange 
experience and strategies.

column7:
Strengthened management capacity 
of state departments and municipal 
agencies
• 	Increased	responsiveness	of	
management and staff to gender 
differences in needs and priorities
• 	Improved	data	and	skills	for	 
gender responsive policy and 
program development
column8:
• 	Do	the	information	systems	of	
the agency generate the sex-
disaggregated data required for 
analyses of needs, options, and 
outcomes (e.g., data on use of  
public transport or managers of 
market stalls)?
• 	Do	the	agency’s	criteria	for	
infrastructure choices or designs 
include attention to how they 
affect women’s safety (e.g., role of 
streetlighting, bus bays, pedestrian 
walkways, protected access to  
public toilets)?
column9:
• 	Allocate	resources	and	expertise	
to improving data systems so they 
generate sex-disaggregated data, and 
to improving analytic skills among 
planners for use of such data.
• 	Assist	partner	state	or	municipal	
agencies to develop linkages with 
research and advocacy organizations 
concerned with urban women’s 
issues (to provide training, feedback, 
research inputs, etc.).

participation in consultation 
processes (related to, for

National Road Safety 
Strategic Action Plan
column19:
• 	The	aim	is	to	reduce	road	accidents	and	casualties	
through the implementation of adequately 
resourced national and local multi-sectoral  
plans under the guidance of the National Road 
Safety Council.
column20:
• 	The	road	safety	policy	focuses	on	
local awareness creation, improving 
the quality of life of the poor 
without mentioning women. This 
can be expanded to include women 
and girls.

column19:
• 	This	is	formulated	in	light	of	the	government’s	
pledge to establish a transport system that is 
safe, cheap, modern, technologically dependable, 
environmentally friendly, and acceptable 
considering globalization.
• 	This	is	prepared	with	a	long	term	30-year	vision	
to highlight the role of transport in economic 
activities and to support continued economic and 
social development.
column20:
• 	Future	policies	have	scope	to	be	
more gender sensitive and address 
some of issues flagged in this policy.

column19:
• 	This	is	commissioned	by	the	Dhaka	Transport	
Coordination Authority and focused 
predominantly on developing strategies for 
building new infrastructure, including rail 
transit, bus rapid transit (BRT), and highway 
development.
• 	The	preferred	strategy	called	for	short-term	
investment in a BRT-based mass transit system 
together with the gradual development of a metro 
rail system. BRT is a “high-quality bus-based 
transit system that delivers fast, comfortable, and 
cost-effective services at metro- level capacities 
through the provision of dedicated lanes, with 
bus ways and iconic stations typically aligned to 
the program of the road, off-board fare collection, 
and fast and frequent operations. Because BRT 
contains features similar to a light rail or metro 
system, it is much more reliable, convenient and 
faster than regular bus services.”a
• 	This	encompasses	a	road	management	program	
that includes the removal of inappropriate road 
users such as vendors using road space, and 
improvements in the operational practices  
of drivers.
• 	Recommendations	of	this	policy	include	the	
(i) consolidation of the reforms in the bus and 
rickshaw industries, (ii) improvement of safety 
measures in pedestrian facilities, (iii) institutional 
strengthening and capacity building, and 
(iv) establishment of a new unitary authority to 
integrate land use and transport planning at the 
strategic level.
column20:
• 	Along	with	the	policy,	the	BRT	
is now being implemented with 
gender issues appropriately 
addressed through pilot projects 
that improve walkability and 
safety (e.g., streetlights, dedicated 
bus seating for women, reserved 
commercial spaces for women at

column60:
a  Completion rate is the percentage of students completing the last year of 
primary school. It is calculated by taking the total number of students in the 
last grade of primary school, minus the number of repeaters in that grade, 
divided by the total number of children of official graduation age.
b   Dropout rate is based on the number of students who leave school for 
any reason before graduation or before completion of a program without 
transferring to another elementary or secondary school.
c  Survival rate is percentage of a cohort of pupils (or students) enrolled in the 
first grade of a given level or cycle of education in a given school year who are 
expected to reach successive grades.
d  Coefficient of internal efficiency is the ideal (optimal) number of pupil-years 
required (i.e., in the absence of repetition and dropout) to produce a number 
of graduates from a given school-cohort for a cycle or level of education 
expressed as a percentage of the actual number of pupil-years spent to 
produce the same number of graduates.

column220:
In Canada, gender equality is a joint responsibility of federal, provincial, and territorial 
governments with a proper coordination and engagement mechanism. Since 1995, the 
federal government has committed to gender-based analysis of legislation, policies, 
and programs, making it mandatory for all Cabinet proposals in 2015. In Budget 2017, 
Canada introduced its first Gender Statement, assessing budget measures through a 
gender lens.

France's 2014 Organic Law on Gender Equality made gender budgeting a key part of 
policymaking, requiring gender impact assessments for all new laws. It also introduced 
quotas for women in senior positions in the civil service, politics, and private sector. 
Since 2010, the annual Budget Law has included an annex on gender equality, outlining 
gender-disaggregated fiscal allocations. These measures ensure that public spending 
and policies actively promote gender equality.

The German federal government views gender equality as a core policy objective and 
has integrated it into budget-making. Since 2000, it has been a guiding principle in the 
Joint  Rules  of  Procedure  of 
the  Federal  Ministries. 
Implementation  has  been 
particularly strong at the subnational level in which Berlin being a leading example.

Italy  has  enacted  gender  equality  laws  at  both  local  and  national  levels,  with  the 
national budget funding initiatives in maternal care, daycare, women’s employment 
incentives,  and  combating  domestic  violence.  A  2016 
legislative  decree  on  State 
budget reform introduced gender budgeting on a trial basis at the national level.

The 
Japanese  government  has  promoted  gender  equality 
through 
legislative 
measures,  including  the  Basic  Act  for  Gender  Equality  of  1999.  It  recently  formally 
adopted  gender  budgeting  to  integrate  gender  perspectives  into  fiscal  policies. Key 
priorities include enhancing women's participation in policymaking and employment, 
improving work-life balance, and reducing poverty. The government also focuses on 
advancing women's education and health to foster long-term gender equity.

The UK has integrated gender equality into fiscal policy through various initiatives. Key 
achievements 
include 
increasing  women's 
participation 
in 
employment 
and 
entrepreneurship. Policies have also focused on creating a supportive environment for 
working  mothers.  These  measures  aim  to  promote  economic  opportunities  and 
financial independence for women.

In  the  U.S.,  recent  legislation  has  aimed  to  combat  violence  against  women  and 
increase female representation in economic and technical leadership roles. However, 
the U.S. remains one of seven countries that has not ratified the UN Convention on 
the  Elimination  of  All  Forms  of  Discrimination  against  Women  (CEDAW).  At  the 
subnational level, San Francisco's gender budgeting initiative focuses on prioritizing 
women's needs in public services and improving infrastructure, particularly for safe 
lighting.
